facts.motto: Alki (a Chinook Jargon word meaning "By and By")
facts.name_origin: Named for President George Washington by the act of Congress that created Washington Territory in 1853. The territory was first going to be called "Columbia," but that name was too close to the District of Columbia. Washington is the only state named after a president.

government.chambers: Washington State Senate (49 senators, 4-year terms) and House of Representatives (98 representatives, 2-year terms); each of the 49 legislative districts elects one senator and two representatives
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), who heads the executive branch along with other statewide elected officials
government.courts: Washington Supreme Court (9 justices, elected statewide or appointed by the governor to fill openings; at least five must agree to decide a case). It meets in Olympia. Below it are the Court of Appeals and superior courts serving all 39 counties.
government.local: 39 counties and 281 incorporated cities and towns.
government.constitution: The Constitution of the State of Washington of 1889 is the state's one and only official constitution. An earlier draft from 1878 was never approved by Congress but helped shape the 1889 version.
government.kid_line: "All political power is inherent in the people, and governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and are established to protect and maintain individual rights." (Washington Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: A people of the Olympic Peninsula, in the northwest corner of the state, whose world revolved around the sea and land; long ago they lived in five main winter villages. Whaling and whales are central to Makah culture, and their canoe journeys continue today.

long_ago.nation: Coast Salish peoples of Puget Sound (such as the Duwamish, Suquamish, Nisqually, and Puyallup)
long_ago.about: Puget Sound nations lived mainly on salmon, halibut, shellfish, and whale. They used cedar to build longhouses and large canoes and made clothing from cedar bark.

A people of the Columbia River Plateau who hunted and gathered and were well known for trading salmon from the yearly runs on the Columbia River. They met the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1805 or 1806 where the Yakima and Columbia Rivers join.

long_ago.nation: Plateau peoples (such as the Spokane, Cayuse, Nez Perce, Palouse, Wenatchee, and Okanogan)
long_ago.about: East of the Cascades, Plateau nations lived by seasonal hunting, fishing, and gathering, with men and women providing equal parts of the food supply.

Nations along the Columbia River became the richest in the region by controlling Celilo Falls, historically the richest salmon fishing place in the Northwest. Other principal coastal nations included the Chinook, Lummi, Quinault, Quileute, and Snohomish.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
today.about: Federally recognized; headquartered in Toppenish, with the state's largest reservation.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
today.about: Federally recognized; based in Nespelem in Ferry and Okanogan Counties.
Federally recognized; about 1,500 people live in and around Neah Bay on the Olympic Peninsula.
Federally recognized; a signer of the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek, living near the Nisqually River.
Federally recognized; also a signer of the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek, whose nations lived around the head of Puget Sound.
Federally recognized; the tribe of Chief Seattle (Si'ahl), whose Suquamish Museum tells the story of Old Man House, a huge longhouse.
Federally recognized; listed by the Governor's Office of Indian Affairs.
Federally recognized; one of the Plateau nations east of the Cascades.

first_peoples.today_note: There are 29 federally recognized tribes in Washington, mostly in Western Washington, and other groups without federal recognition. The Governor's Office of Indian Affairs lists them, including the Lummi Nation, Quinault Indian Nation, Cowlitz Indian Tribe, Muckleshoot Indian Tribe, and Snoqualmie Indian Tribe.
sites: Makah Museum (Makah Cultural and Research Center), Neah Bay: holds artifacts 300 to 500 years old from the Ozette village, which a mudslide buried; more than 50,000 well-preserved artifacts have been found
Yakama Nation Cultural Heritage Center, Toppenish: life-size dwellings of the Plateau People
Suquamish Museum: exhibits on the Suquamish people, the boarding school experience, and Old Man House
Duwamish Longhouse and Cultural Center, Seattle: a traditional Puget Salish cedar post longhouse

history.event: The skeleton known as Kennewick Man, one of the oldest and most complete human skeletons found in North America, dates to this time; it was found in Washington in 1996.
About 125 distinct Northwest nations speaking about 50 languages and dialects live in the region, fishing for salmon, building cedar longhouses and canoes, and trading at places like Celilo Falls.
A mudslide, perhaps set off by an earthquake about 500 years ago, buries part of the Makah village at Ozette. In 1700 a huge Cascadia megathrust earthquake strikes the coast.
Spanish captain Bruno de Heceta makes the first recorded European landing on the Washington coast, near today's Point Grenville. A smallpox epidemic in the 1770s devastates Native nations.
British explorer George Vancouver explores the straits. American captain Robert Gray, who found the mouth of the Columbia River and named it after his ship, begins trading sea otter furs.
The Lewis and Clark Expedition enters what is now Washington on October 10.
Missionary Marcus Whitman builds a mission among the Cayuse near Walla Walla. Many Cayuse die from new diseases, and in 1847 some Cayuse kill Whitman and twelve others, starting the Cayuse War.

Black pioneer George Washington Bush and his wife Isabella James Bush lead settlers to found New Market (now Tumwater), avoiding Oregon's law excluding Black people. Britain gives up its claims south of the 49th parallel in the Oregon Treaty.
Congress creates Washington Territory on March 2.

Territorial governor Isaac Stevens pressures nations into treaties (Medicine Creek, Point Elliott, Walla Walla, and others) that take most of their land and move them onto reservations, while promising fishing rights.

War breaks out with the Yakama and Puget Sound nations. Nisqually leader Leschi, who protested the Medicine Creek Treaty, is hanged on February 19, 1858; a state historical court cleared his name in 2004.
Anti-Chinese mobs force Tacoma's Chinese community, which had numbered about 700 people, out of the city; on November 3 the last 150 to 200 residents are rounded up and marched to the train station.
Washington adopts its constitution and becomes the 42nd state on November 11.

trailblazers.name: Chief Seattle (Si'ahl)
trailblazers.text: Si'ahl led the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples and chose a path of working with the new settlers. He was the first to sign the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott, which gave up about 2.5 million acres of land. The city of Seattle is named after him.

trailblazers.name: George Washington Bush
trailblazers.text: George Bush and his wife Isabella helped lead settlers north of the Columbia River in 1846 and founded New Market, now Tumwater. Oregon's laws kept Black people out, so the territorial legislature later asked Congress to give the Bushes clear ownership of their farm, which it did in 1855, making him one of the first Black landowners in Washington.

trailblazers.name: Bertha Knight Landes
trailblazers.text: Bertha Knight Landes served on the Seattle City Council and became the first woman mayor of a major American city, leading Seattle from 1926 to 1928.

trailblazers.name: Gordon Hirabayashi
trailblazers.text: Born in Seattle, Gordon Hirabayashi refused to obey the World War II curfew and removal orders aimed at Japanese Americans. In 1942 he turned himself in to the FBI to challenge the orders in court; his convictions were overturned in 1986 and 1987, and he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

trailblazers.name: Wing Luke
trailblazers.text: Born in Guangdong, China, Wing Luke became an assistant state attorney general for civil rights. In 1962 he became the first Asian American elected to office in the Pacific Northwest and the first person of color on the Seattle City Council. The Wing Luke Museum is named for him.

trailblazers.name: Billy Frank Jr.
trailblazers.text: Billy Frank Jr. was first arrested at age 14 for fishing for salmon on the Nisqually River. He led "fish-ins" to defend treaty fishing rights. In 1974 a U.S. District Court judge, George Boldt, ruled that treaty tribes were entitled to 50 percent of the catch (the Boldt Decision), and the U.S. Supreme Court largely upheld it in 1979. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.

trailblazers.name: Roberto Maestas
trailblazers.text: Roberto Maestas, born in rural New Mexico, helped farm workers organize in the Yakima Valley and started an English-learning program in Seattle. In 1972 he and other activists occupied an empty school on Beacon Hill, which became El Centro de la Raza, a community center.

landforms: Cascade Range with volcanoes Mount Baker, Glacier Peak, Mount Rainier (highest point, 14,410 feet), Mount St. Helens, and Mount Adams
Okanogan Highlands, Kettle River Range, and Selkirk Mountains
geography.regions: The Cascade Range splits the state into wet, forested Western Washington (the Olympic Peninsula, Pacific coast, and Puget Sound lowlands) and dry Eastern Washington (the Columbia Plateau, the Okanogan Highlands, and the Palouse).

ecosystems.name: Temperate rainforest (Olympic Peninsula)
ecosystems.about: The western Olympic Peninsula gets up to 160 inches of rain a year, the wettest area of the lower 48 states. Forests like the Hoh Rainforest are among the only rainforests in the continental United States.

ecosystems.name: Puget Sound and the salmon rivers
ecosystems.about: Salmon, halibut, shellfish, and whales fed coastal nations for thousands of years, and millions of salmon once passed Celilo Falls on the Columbia to spawn. The orca is the state marine mammal.

ecosystems.name: Shrub-steppe and grassland (Columbia Plateau)
ecosystems.about: In the rain shadow east of the Cascades, some places get only 6 inches of rain a year, so dry grassland, shrub-steppe, and dunes replace forests.

ecosystems.name: Alpine mountains and glaciers
ecosystems.about: Mount Rainier is covered with more glacial ice than any other peak in the lower 48 states. The Olympic marmot lives only in Washington and is the state land mammal.

science.weather: West of the Cascades, winters are cloudy and rainy with mild temperatures; east of the Cascades is dry and semi-arid. Mount Baker set a world record in 1999 with 1,140 inches of snow in a single season. Hazards include active volcanoes, large earthquakes (a giant Cascadia megathrust earthquake struck in 1700), and dust storms in dry farm areas.
science.resources: Washington is a leading lumber producer and the largest U.S. producer of apples, hops, pears, blueberries, spearmint oil, and sweet cherries, and it grows lots of wheat. Fishing (salmon, halibut), wine, and aircraft and shipbuilding are also big parts of the economy.
science.highlight: On May 18, 1980, after weeks of small quakes, the north side of Mount St. Helens slid away in the largest landslide in recorded history and the volcano erupted. The blast flattened forests up to 12 miles away, killed 57 people, and spread ash across Washington and nearby states.

g3_ss.title: Washington's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Olympia, Seattle, and the student's town; learn the Legislature (Senate and House), the governor, and the Supreme Court; read Article I, Section 1.

g3_ss.title: Washington's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Compare Coast Salish and Makah life by the sea with Yakama and Plateau life along the rivers; cedar canoes, salmon, and the 29 federally recognized tribes today.

g3_ss.title: Washington Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Chief Seattle, George Washington Bush, Bertha Knight Landes, Wing Luke, and Billy Frank Jr.; students make a trailblazer trading card for each.

g45_ss.title: Washington's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Ozette and the Makah, Celilo Falls and Plateau trade, Coast Salish longhouses; how nations governed and traded before 1775.

g45_ss.title: Explorers, Fur Traders, and Missions
g45_ss.plan: Heceta, Gray, Vancouver, Lewis and Clark, the Hudson's Bay Company, the Whitman mission and Cayuse War, and George Washington Bush's settlement.

g45_ss.title: Treaties to Statehood, 1853–1889
g45_ss.plan: Washington Territory, the Stevens treaties and their promises of fishing rights, Leschi and the wars of 1855–1858, the 1885 expulsion of Chinese Americans, and statehood in 1889.

g3_sci.title: Rainforest and Rain Shadow
g3_sci.plan: Why the Olympic Peninsula is so wet and the Columbia Plateau so dry; a simple model of mountains blocking rain clouds.

g3_sci.title: Salmon Journeys
g3_sci.plan: Salmon life cycle from river to ocean and back; why salmon matter to orcas, people, and forests.

g3_sci.title: Washington's Volcanoes
g3_sci.plan: Meet the five big Cascade volcanoes; how scientists watch Mount Rainier and Mount St. Helens to keep people safe.

g45_sci.title: The 1980 Eruption of Mount St. Helens
g45_sci.plan: Plate tectonics, the bulging north face, the landslide and blast, and how the land and living things have recovered since.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers and Earthquakes of the Cascades
g45_sci.plan: Mount Rainier's glacial ice, the Cascadia subduction zone, the 1700 earthquake, and preparing for quakes.

g45_sci.title: Ecosystems East and West
g45_sci.plan: Compare temperate rainforest and shrub-steppe food webs; investigate the Olympic marmot, Western hemlock, and how irrigation changed Eastern Washington farming.
